blocks.text: Asked to touch the examiner's finger and then his own nose, a 55-year-old man swings his left hand past the target, corrects, overshoots again, and develops a tremor that gets worse as the fingertip approaches. His strength and sensation are normal. The movement is intact; its accuracy is not.

blocks.markdown:
The **cerebellum** compares the **intended** movement (from the cortex) with the **actual** movement (from proprioceptive and vestibular feedback) and corrects errors, so that movement is smooth, accurate and well timed. It also contributes to balance, posture, motor learning and, to a lesser degree, cognition. It does not initiate movement and does not cause weakness when damaged.

**Structure.** The cerebellum has a midline **vermis**, two **hemispheres** (with an **intermediate zone** next to the vermis and a **lateral zone**), and the **flocculonodular lobe**. The cortex has three layers; **Purkinje cells** are its only output and are **GABAergic**, inhibiting the **deep cerebellar nuclei** (**dentate, emboliform and globose** (together the interposed nuclei), and **fastigial**), which carry the output from the cerebellum. Connections run through three **peduncles**: the **inferior** (mainly input from the spinal cord, vestibular system and olivary nucleus), the **middle** (input from the pontine nuclei, entirely afferent) and the **superior** (the main output, to the thalamus and red nucleus, and also carries the ventral spinocerebellar tract).

rows: Vestibular nuclei (via fastigial route in part)
Fastigial and interposed nuclei to brainstem and thalamus
Posture, trunk and limb movement and tone
Cerebral cortex via pontine nuclei and middle cerebellar peduncle
Dentate nucleus to contralateral ventral lateral thalamus and motor cortex
Planning and timing of skilled movement

blocks.title: Somatotopy of lesions
blocks.text: Midline (vermis and flocculonodular) lesions affect the trunk, posture, gait and eye movements. Hemisphere lesions affect the limbs, with lateral hemisphere lesions disrupting coordinated skilled limb movement on the same side.

blocks.markdown: **Signs of a cerebellar hemisphere lesion** are remembered as **DANISH**: **D**ysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements); **A**taxia (incoordinated limb movement, and gait ataxia with a wide base); **N**ystagmus; **I**ntention tremor (tremor that increases as the limb approaches its target) and dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting, 'past-pointing'); **S**lurred or scanning speech (dysarthria); **H**ypotonia. Signs are **ipsilateral** to the lesion. A **vermis** lesion typically causes **truncal ataxia** with a wide-based, staggering gait and relative sparing of the limbs.

blocks.title: Why a left hemisphere lesion gives left-sided signs
blocks.prompt: Explain why a lesion of the left cerebellar hemisphere causes incoordination of the left arm, using a double-crossing argument.

steps.text: Cortical motor plans reach the left cerebellar hemisphere from the right motor cortex: the corticopontine fibres synapse in the pontine nuclei and the pontocerebellar fibres cross the midline and enter the left hemisphere through the middle cerebellar peduncle. That is crossing 1.

The left dentate nucleus sends output through the superior cerebellar peduncle, which decussates in the midbrain to reach the right ventral lateral thalamus and right red nucleus. That is crossing 2, so the signal returns to the right motor cortex, the cortex from which the plan came.
The right corticospinal tract then crosses at the pyramidal decussation to act on the left side of the body. That is crossing 3.

blocks.answer: The left cerebellar hemisphere influences the right motor cortex (crossing in the superior cerebellar peduncle), and the right corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramids to the left limbs. The pathway thus returns to the side of the cerebellar hemisphere, so a left hemisphere lesion causes left-sided signs.

blocks.title: Localising by pattern
blocks.prompt: A 6-year-old child has progressive unsteadiness, falls backwards when sitting unsupported, and walks with a wide base. Finger-nose testing is normal. Which part of the cerebellum is most likely involved?

steps.text: Truncal instability when sitting unsupported and a wide-based gait indicate failure of midline axial control.
Normal finger-nose testing means the limb (hemisphere) circuits are largely spared.
Midline axial control is served by the vermis (spinocerebellum), and vestibulocerebellar structures close to the midline.

blocks.answer: The midline vermis. A midline cerebellar mass in a child is typical of a medulloblastoma, which is a teaching example here.

items: Cerebellar lesions cause incoordination (ataxia), not weakness or sensory loss.
Signs are ipsilateral to a cerebellar hemisphere lesion because of the double decussation.
Hypotonia and pendular reflexes reflect reduced facilitation of motor neurones.
Chronic alcohol use and some drugs and toxins selectively damage the vermis, producing wide-based gait ataxia with relative sparing of the arms.

blocks.title: Intention versus rest tremor
blocks.text: Cerebellar tremor increases as the target is approached (intention tremor) and is absent at rest. The rest tremor of Parkinson disease is present at rest and diminishes on movement. They arise from different circuits.

blocks.title: Ataxia and dysmetria
blocks.text: Ataxia is incoordination of movement not due to weakness or sensory loss. Dysmetria is the specific error of misjudging the range of a movement, so that the limb overshoots or undershoots its target.

points: The cerebellum compares intended and actual movement; Purkinje cells are GABAergic and inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei.

The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) controls balance and eye movement, the spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zone) posture and limb movement, and the cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) planning of skilled movement.
Hemisphere lesions produce ipsilateral dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria and hypotonia; vermis lesions cause truncal ataxia.
Signs are ipsilateral because the cerebellar pathways decussate twice in the pathway and the corticospinal tract crosses again.

questions.stem: Which functional division of the cerebellum corresponds to the flocculonodular lobe?

options.text: Vestibulocerebellum, controlling balance and eye movements

questions.correctOptionText: Vestibulocerebellum, controlling balance and eye movements

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the flocculonodular lobe connects with the vestibular nuclei.
distractorRationale.b: The spinocerebellum is the vermis and intermediate zone.
distractorRationale.c: The cerebrocerebellum is the lateral hemisphere.
distractorRationale.d: The cerebellum is not a primary pain centre.

questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe has reciprocal connections with the vestibular apparatus and nuclei, and mediates balance and vestibulo-ocular function.

questions.stem: Which deep cerebellar nucleus is the principal output of the lateral hemisphere to the contralateral ventral lateral thalamus?

distractorRationale.a: The fastigial nucleus serves the vermis and vestibular system.
distractorRationale.b: The globose nucleus is part of the interposed nuclei serving the intermediate zone.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the dentate nucleus serves the lateral hemisphere.
distractorRationale.d: The red nucleus lies in the midbrain, not the cerebellum.

questions.explanation: The lateral hemisphere projects to the dentate nucleus, which sends fibres through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral ventral lateral thalamus and then the motor cortex.

questions.stem: Which cerebellar peduncle carries input from the pontine nuclei to the cerebellum?

distractorRationale.a: The superior peduncle is the main output pathway.
distractorRationale.b: The inferior peduncle carries spinal, vestibular and olivary input.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the middle peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibres.
distractorRationale.d: The cerebral peduncle is a midbrain structure.

questions.explanation: Pontine nuclei relay cortical information to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere through the middle cerebellar peduncle, which is entirely afferent.

questions.stem: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurones of the cerebellar cortex. What is their effect on their target neurones?

options.text: Inhibitory, via GABA, onto deep cerebellar nuclei

questions.correctOptionText: Inhibitory, via GABA, onto deep cerebellar nuclei

distractorRationale.c: Purkinje cells do not release ACh.

questions.explanation: Purkinje cells release GABA onto neurones of the deep cerebellar nuclei. The cerebellar cortex therefore shapes the output of the nuclei by inhibition.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has a tremor of her right hand that is absent at rest and worsens as she brings a glass to her mouth. Which sign is this?

distractorRationale.a: A rest tremor is present at rest and is typical of Parkinson disease.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a tremor increasing towards the target is cerebellar.
distractorRationale.c: Fasciculations are brief muscle twitches from lower motor neurone disease.
distractorRationale.d: Chorea is irregular, flowing movement not linked to the target.

questions.explanation: A tremor that is absent at rest and increases during goal-directed movement is an intention tremor, a cerebellar sign. A rest tremor would diminish with movement.

questions.stem: True or false: cerebellar hemisphere disease typically causes reduced muscle tone (hypotonia) rather than weakness.
questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia and incoordination but not paralysis, since corticospinal pathways remain intact. The cerebellum modulates rather than initiates movement.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who has drunk heavily for decades has a wide-based staggering gait. Heel-to-shin testing is mildly abnormal but finger-nose testing is normal and his speech is unaffected. Which part of the cerebellum is most affected?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: gait ataxia with relative sparing of the arms localises to the midline.
distractorRationale.b: Lateral hemisphere disease would impair finger-nose testing.
distractorRationale.c: Deep nuclei lesions cause widespread limb and speech signs.
distractorRationale.d: Peduncular lesions are uncommon in alcohol-related degeneration.

questions.explanation: A wide-based gait with normal arm coordination indicates midline vermian involvement, which is the typical pattern in alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration of the anterior superior vermis.

questions.stem: An infarct involves the right cerebellar hemisphere. On which side will limb ataxia appear?

options.text: Neither, because the cerebellum does not control limbs

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ipsilateral signs result from double decussation.
distractorRationale.b: This would be true of a cortical lesion, not a cerebellar one.
distractorRationale.c: Hemisphere lesions are unilateral in effect.
distractorRationale.d: The cerebellar hemispheres coordinate the ipsilateral limbs.

questions.explanation: The cerebellar pathways to and from the cortex cross twice, and the corticospinal tract crosses once more, so each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the limbs on its own side.

questions.stem: Contrast the side of the body affected by an infarct of the left motor cortex with that of an infarct of the left cerebellar hemisphere, and explain the difference using the decussations involved.
markingGuide: Left motor cortex infarct causes right-sided weakness
Corticospinal tract decussates once, at the pyramids in the caudal medulla
Left cerebellar infarct causes left-sided incoordination (ipsilateral)
Cerebellar loop involves crossing in the pontocerebellar fibres and in the superior cerebellar peduncle, followed by the corticospinal crossing

The cerebellar loop crosses twice (cortex to cerebellum, then cerebellum back to cortex), so the cerebellum acts through the cortex whose corticospinal tract (one crossing) serves the side of the cerebellar lesion
Cerebellar lesion causes ataxia, not paralysis
questions.explanation: A single crossing of the corticospinal tract explains contralateral weakness after a cortical lesion, whereas the cerebellar loop includes additional crossings that restore the ipsilateral relationship. The type of deficit also differs: weakness versus incoordination.

questions.stem: A patient with a right cerebellar hemisphere lesion is examined. List five signs you would expect on the right, define dysdiadochokinesia and dysmetria, and state which functional division of the cerebellum is involved.
markingGuide: Any five of: dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, dysmetria, slurred speech, hypotonia
Dysdiadochokinesia: impaired rapid alternating movements (such as pronation and supination)
Dysmetria: inaccurate range of movement, overshooting or undershooting the target
Involves the spinocerebellum and cerebrocerebellum (intermediate and lateral hemisphere) rather than the vestibulocerebellum alone
questions.explanation: A hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral limb incoordination, with errors in timing (dysdiadochokinesia) and in range (dysmetria). The hemispheres correspond to the intermediate and lateral zones, that is, spinocerebellar and cerebrocerebellar function.
